reason: E2 directly supports that defective T-graphite provides nucleation sites and that nanoparticles intercalate on edge planes, leading to high binding energy and excellent thermal stability, which underpins the anchoring and binding energy premises. However, neither E1 nor E2 provides evidence that HEA composition modulates metal–support binding strength or that this anchoring specifically delays premelting and raises melting temperature; these premises are extrapolations beyond the cited data.
premises: Defect-rich carbon supports (e.g., turbostratic graphite) provide strong anchoring sites for metal nanoparticles
Strong anchoring at defect sites increases the binding energy of surface metal atoms
Increased surface atom binding energy restrains surface diffusion and delays premelting
HEA composition modulates the strength of metal–support interactions at defect sites
Delayed premelting translates to a higher overall melting temperature for supported nanoparticles
